analysis.one_liner: Bars large websites from using manipulative design to extract user data or hook children compulsively.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after referral to a House subcommittee in December 2021, no action was taken before Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The DETOUR Act would prohibit large online operators — websites and services with more than 100 million monthly users — from designing interfaces that trick people into giving consent or personal data, a practice known as "dark patterns." It would require companies to get users' informed consent before running behavioral or psychological experiments on them, disclose experiments publicly every 90 days, and ban designing features for children under 13 that encourage compulsive use. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and industry associations could register as professional standards bodies offering safe harbors for compliant conduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use large online services — social networks, search engines, and email providers with over 100 million users — would gain protections against interfaces designed to obscure or impair their choices, undisclosed behavioral experiments on their activity, and features engineered to keep children compulsively engaged. Users would get 90-day disclosures of experiments involving their data, deletion of data collected without valid consent, and independent review boards overseeing research, with the FTC empowered to penalize violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of the biggest online platforms

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits large online operators from designing or manipulating user interfaces with the purpose or substantial effect of subverting user autonomy, decision-making, or choice in order to obtain consent or user data — the practice known as dark patterns.

Requires informed, affirmative consent before a company segments users into groups for behavioral or psychological experiments, and bars relying on a child's consent or on consent buried in a general service agreement.

Prohibits designing interfaces aimed at children under 13 that encourage compulsive usage, including auto-play video started without the user's consent, and requires companies to disclose behavioral experiments publicly at least every 90 days.

Requires companies running behavioral research to establish independent review boards registered with the FTC, and to delete data obtained through inappropriately acquired consent, with FTC enforcement treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Large online operators — services with more than 100 million monthly users, which describes a small set of major technology firms — would bear the costs: redesigning interfaces to remove manipulative patterns, building 90-day disclosure routines, standing up and registering independent review boards, deleting data from experiments lacking valid consent, and potential FTC penalties. Consumers would pay nothing directly, though some design and testing practices that boost engagement would become costlier or off-limits.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows an association of large online operators to register with the FTC as a professional standards body, and operators that rely in good faith on that body's guidance are shielded from enforcement — a structure that risks letting the regulated industry write the rules it follows.

The standard for 'compulsive usage' is broad, covering behavior causing psychological distress, anxiety, or depression, and the ban reaches any interface 'directed to' children under 13, which could be difficult to apply consistently and could chill ordinary design testing beyond the de minimis safe harbors the bill contemplates.

Compliance would fall entirely on a handful of the largest companies — 90-day disclosure of every engagement experiment, registered review boards with member resumes filed to the FTC, and consent rules for any user segmentation research — costs and administrative burdens the bill imposes only on the biggest platforms rather than the whole market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to hundreds of millions of people who use a small number of dominant platforms every day: clearer choices, consent before being made a research subject, and limits on features engineered to hook children. The costs fall on the same handful of giant firms, which is where a bill like this is supposed to put them. The genuine design flaws are the industry standards-body safe harbor, which hands platforms a route to shape their own compliance guidance, and the vagueness of the 'compulsive usage' standard. Weighed honestly, the consumer protections are substantial and the compliance burden lands on the parties best able to bear it, but the bill's structure would have needed careful FTC rulemaking to keep the industry body from diluting the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and died without ever getting a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Blunt Rochester introduced the bill on November 30, 2021, joined by Rep. Anthony Gonzalez of Ohio as its cosponsor.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and on December 1, 2021, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online platforms came out ahead: the companies with more than 100 million users kept their freedom to use manipulative interface designs, run undisclosed behavioral experiments on their users, and design engagement features for children without any of the restrictions the bill would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition is unknown.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (social media, search, email)
industries.note: The bill would bar platforms with over 100 million users from using manipulative interface designs to extract consent and data, force disclosure of behavioral experiments, and ban compulsive-usage design aimed at children — directly restricting the design and experimentation practices that drive engagement. Its defeat left those practices unrestricted.

Behavioral research on user activity feeds engagement optimization and ad targeting; the bill would require informed consent for segmenting users into research groups, 90-day public disclosure of engagement experiments, and deletion of data gathered without valid consent, raising the cost of these practices.
